title: Oil Just Topped $109. Is It Too Late to Buy Chevron (CVX)? History Has a Clear Answer. - The Motley Fool
content: Every time oil has topped $110/barrel before, the result has been the same. In absolute terms, the difference between a barrel of oil that costs $99 and a barrel of oil that costs $101 isn't much. But psychologically, that difference is immense. At the end of the day on Tuesday, a barrel of benchmark Brent Crude oil cost $99.07, but early this morning, it was going for $101.02. Throughout the day, the price climbed higher, briefly topping $109. As of this writing, the per-barrel price of the global benchmark is over $108. That's bad news for just about everybody... except shares of U.S. oil companies like Chevron (CVX -0.49%) and ExxonMobil (XOM +0.61%). But now that oil has broken through the $100/barrel threshold, is it too late to buy shares of Chevron? Our team of credit card pros don’t just recommend this card—they actually use it. Motley Fool Money calls it a top pick for a reason. Because the war in Iran has been going on for so long, there's plenty of evidence that Chevron's stock is moving in tandem with Brent Crude oil prices. Over the six and a half months of the conflict, the price of Brent Crude has bounced around wildly. It began the war at about $70/barrel, but soared to $109/barrel in early April, slipped to $90/barrel in late April, and peaked at a high of $114/barrel in early May. When our analyst team has a stock tip, it can pay to listen. After all, Stock Advisor’s total average return is 950%* — a market-crushing outperformance compared to 211% for the S&P 500. They just revealed what they believe are the 10 best stocks for investors to buy right now, available when you join Stock Advisor. After a ceasefire agreement was signed in June, the Brent Crude price fell back down to $72/barrel, but it steadily climbed again as the war dragged on through August, and is showing no signs of dropping again. Both Chevron's and ExxonMobil's stock prices have mostly moved in tandem with the Brent Crude price. Their shares surged when Brent Crude prices rose in March, May, July, and August, and dropped when Brent Crude prices fell in April and June. The pattern has been crystal clear. The reason Chevron's share price has risen and fallen in tandem with Brent Crude prices during the war is that the vast majority of Chevron's production is located outside the Middle East. Aside from a small amount of onshore production in the Partitioned Zone between Kuwait and Saudi Arabia, Chevron doesn't have any production operations in the Persian Gulf. Its main oil production operations are in the U.S., Kazakhstan, and Argentina, none of which are directly affected by the war in Iran. This allows Chevron to benefit from higher global oil prices driven by Middle East supply disruptions while still producing plenty of oil to sell at those inflated prices. Unfortunately for would-be Chevron investors, if the historical pattern holds, it is probably too late to squeeze much short-term gain out of the current situation by buying Chevron stock. With Brent Crude prices already above $108/barrel, they're approaching the peak levels we saw in March and May. And after those short-lived peaks, Chevron's stock declined sharply, dropping 13% from its March high by mid-April, and 16% from its May high by early July. Today, Chevron's stock is up 28.4% from that July low and trading at an all-time high. Historically speaking, oil prices have rarely moved above $110/barrel. Even when they have, they've hardly ever stayed at that level for long. The longest sustained period in history during which Brent Crude prices remained above $110/barrel lasted only three months (Feb. through April of 2012). In other words, for oil prices to go up from here and stay up for longer than three months would constitute a never-before-seen historical anomaly. But that's the only way Chevron's stock would go up significantly in the short term, if the historical patterns hold. Historical anomalies do sometimes happen, but betting on them is a risky investment strategy. Instead, investors should expect Chevron's share price to decline along with oil prices in the near future. Exactly how soon it will happen, though, is anyone's guess. The move placed energy among the only sectors posting gains during a session where broader equity gauges slipped and Treasury yields climbed toward multiyear highs. Chevron, one of the largest integrated majors listed on the New York Stock Exchange, has drawn heightened attention as crude markets swing sharply, given its diversified upstream base spanning North America, Central Asia, and international joint ventures, alongside a refining and chemicals footprint that rounds out its earnings profile. The session also unfolded against the broader S&P 500 backdrop, keeping the company's move in a wider U.S. equity-market context. Brent crude, the global benchmark most closely tied to seaborne trade flows, pushed through a ceiling that had held for a stretch of years, a move traders tied directly to escalating friction around the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway carrying a substantial share of the world's seaborne crude and liquefied natural gas. West Texas Intermediate also pushed sharply higher, narrowing the spread that traders watch closely when assessing relative strength between international and domestic crude grades. Energy desks described trading volumes as elevated, with options markets pricing continued swings as headlines out of the Gulf region evolved through the session, a pattern that has repeated through the summer months as shipping-corridor tensions have flared intermittently. The Strait of Hormuz has moved to the center of market attention as reports of disrupted tanker traffic and heightened naval activity spread through wire services and energy trading desks. The corridor separates the Persian Gulf from the Gulf of Oman and functions as the primary maritime artery for crude and liquefied natural gas moving from major Gulf producers toward Asian and European buyers. Chevron maintains joint-venture positions in the broader Middle East region, giving the company both direct and indirect exposure to conditions along the corridor. Energy strategists have noted that even the perception of elevated exposure along the corridor tends to add a meaningful premium to crude pricing, independent of whether physical flows are actually interrupted. Chevron holds one of the largest acreage positions in the Permian Basin among the integrated majors, a footprint that has become central to the company's near-term production growth strategy. Efficiency gains from longer laterals, enhanced completion techniques, and continued infrastructure buildout have allowed the company to grow Permian output while maintaining capital discipline across the broader portfolio. The current price environment, with West Texas Intermediate trading well above levels seen earlier in the year, has renewed conversations across the basin about whether operators will lean back toward growth-oriented spending or continue prioritizing free cash flow generation and stockholder distributions, a balance Chevron management has emphasized repeatedly in recent public commentary. Beyond North America, Chevron's position in Kazakhstan through the Tengizchevroil joint venture represents one of the largest single sources of international upstream growth across the company's portfolio. A major expansion project at the Tengiz field has been ramping production, adding barrels that diversify Chevron's supply base away from a singular reliance on Gulf Coast or Permian output. The Kazakhstan position also carries its own set of logistical considerations, given the export routes required to move crude from a landlocked production base to international markets, a dynamic that market watchers weigh alongside Gulf-corridor exposure when assessing the company's overall supply-chain sensitivity. Chevron has moved to expand operations in Venezuela, targeting a substantial increase in production as part of a broader push to grow output across its international portfolio. The expansion reflects a broader repositioning within the company's upstream strategy, which has increasingly emphasized growth openings in the Middle East, Central Asia, and Latin America alongside its core Permian Basin position. Market watchers have flagged the Venezuela expansion as a notable step given the historically complex operating environment in the country, with the move seen as part of a broader effort to squeeze additional output from established international assets while pursuing new growth avenues in domestic shale and power generation. Chevron's downstream operations, spanning refining and chemicals, provide a partial offset to swings in upstream earnings tied to crude pricing, though refining margins can compress when product prices lag feedstock costs during sharp crude rallies. The company has also signaled growing interest in power generation, including projects aimed at supplying electricity to data-center and industrial customers, a diversification move that market watchers have described as an emerging growth avenue beyond traditional hydrocarbon production. Executives have framed the power generation push as complementary to the core energy portfolio rather than a wholesale shift away from oil and natural gas production. Chevron has maintained a conservative balance sheet relative to many industry peers, an approach that has allowed the company to sustain its distribution program and fund buybacks even through periods of softer crude pricing. That balance sheet strength has become a differentiator during periods of crude volatility, giving management room to weigh additional buybacks, project sanctioning, or further debt reduction without compromising the distribution program that has made the stock a mainstay among stockholders seeking durable payouts from the energy patch. The company's chief financial officer recently described the company as operating from a stronger position than in prior cycles, citing the diversified asset base and disciplined spending approach. Chevron has maintained a long-running distribution growth streak, a track record that has continued through multiple cyclical downturns in crude pricing. Alongside the distribution, the company has run a sizable buyback program funded by free cash flow generated across its integrated operations. Market participants tracking the broader Oil and Gas Stocks landscape have noted that the combination of a resilient distribution and an active buyback program has made integrated majors a preferred destination for capital rotating into the sector during episodes of crude strength, particularly when other parts of the market are contending with softer conditions tied to elevated Treasury yields. Global supply dynamics remain in flux as the coalition of producers known as OPEC+ continues to calibrate output in response to both the Gulf tensions and broader demand signals from major consuming economies. Market watchers across trading desks have flagged that any further escalation along the Strait of Hormuz could prompt a more aggressive response from major producers seeking to offset lost barrels, while a de-escalation could just as quickly unwind much of the recent price premium. Chevron, alongside its integrated peers, monitors these production-strategy shifts closely given the direct bearing they have on realized pricing across its global portfolio. Chevron competes with a set of integrated majors and independent producers that collectively make up the Oil and Gas Stocks landscape, including Exxon Mobil, ConocoPhillips, and Occidental Petroleum, each carrying a distinct mix of upstream, midstream, and downstream exposure. The integrated structure that Chevron maintains, spanning production through refining, chemicals, and an emerging power generation business, differentiates its earnings profile from pure-play upstream operators that carry more direct leverage to crude pricing swings. That structural difference has been evident in trading patterns this week, as the integrated majors have shown somewhat more measured moves relative to some of the pure-play producers. Chevron remains one of the largest components of the Oil and Gas Stocks category by market capitalization and carries meaningful weight within the, meaning swings in the stock have an outsized bearing on index performance during sessions when energy diverges sharply from the rest of the market, as it has this week. The stock's behavior is closely watched not only by market participants focused on the energy patch but also by those tracking the broader index, given how few sectors posted gains during a session dominated by climbing Treasury yields and a firmer dollar. Even as crude prices surge, the broader industry continues to contend with longer-horizon pressures tied to the energy transition, including growing electric-vehicle adoption in key demand markets, tightening emissions rules across multiple jurisdictions, and continued scrutiny of capital spending decisions from stockholders weighing near-term cash generation against longer-term positioning. Chevron has responded by expanding its lower-carbon initiatives, including carbon capture and hydrogen pilots, while maintaining that traditional hydrocarbon production will remain central to its portfolio for a considerable stretch of time given continued demand growth in emerging economies. Chevron carries meaningful natural gas exposure through domestic Permian Basin production and international positions, including a stake in liquefied natural gas export capacity that ties the company's earnings to global gas pricing alongside crude. Global gas markets have tightened alongside crude this week, with Asian and European buyers competing for cargoes amid the same shipping-corridor tensions weighing on crude flows through the Strait of Hormuz. The liquefied natural gas business has become an increasingly important growth avenue for the company, complementing crude and providing a further channel through which elevated global energy pricing feeds into overall earnings across the diversified portfolio. Chevron has heavily in data analytics, automated drilling techniques, and digital monitoring systems across its Permian and Kazakhstan operations, aiming to lower per-barrel costs and improve well performance over time. These efficiency gains have become a differentiator during periods when capital discipline limits the pace of new project sanctioning, allowing the company to extract additional value from existing acreage rather than relying solely on new development spending. Executives have repeatedly pointed to these technology-driven efficiency gains as a structural advantage that supports margins even when crude pricing moderates from current elevated levels. Market watchers have drawn comparisons between the current episode of Strait of Hormuz tension and prior periods of Middle East disruption that produced sharp, sometimes short-lived, crude price spikes. History indicates that while geopolitical shocks tied to the corridor can produce swift and pronounced moves in crude benchmarks, the durability of those moves often hinges on whether physical flows are actually interrupted for a sustained stretch or whether the premium reflects mainly the perception of exposure. Chevron's diversified global portfolio, spanning multiple producing regions outside the immediate Gulf corridor, has historically provided a partial buffer against the sharpest swings tied to any single geopolitical flashpoint. Chevron operates a wide-reaching refining and marketing network across the United States and international markets, with fuel brands recognized by drivers across many regions and a logistics footprint spanning pipelines, marine terminals, and storage assets. That downstream and midstream reach gives the company a further channel of earnings that moves somewhat independently of upstream production volumes, particularly during periods when crude pricing swings sharply and refining margins adjust with a lag. The marketing network also provides a stable base of cash generation that complements the more cyclical upstream segment, supporting the company's ability to sustain distributions and buybacks through periods of crude volatility such as the current episode tied to the Strait of Hormuz. Executives have periodically highlighted the marketing and logistics network as an underappreciated stabilizer within the broader portfolio, noting that it helps smooth earnings across the commodity cycle even when upstream results swing sharply on crude price moves tied to geopolitical developments in the Gulf region and elsewhere. The refining network also allows Chevron to capture value from a wide slate of crude grades, including barrels sourced from its own upstream operations as well as third-party supply, giving the company flexibility to optimize feedstock costs even as benchmark pricing swings sharply. Storage and marine terminal assets tied to the logistics network provide additional optionality during periods of shipping-corridor disruption, allowing the company to reroute cargoes and manage inventory positions with greater flexibility than producers lacking comparable downstream infrastructure. That flexibility has taken on added relevance this week as market participants weigh the prospects for continued disruption along the Strait of Hormuz corridor and its knock-on effects for crude and refined product flows across the broader Gulf region and beyond. title: ExxonMobil Stock at a Premium: Opportunity or Reason to Stay Cautious? - The Globe and Mail
content: ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation XOM is trading at a premium, meaning investors are willing to pay more for the stock. On a relative basis, the stock is trading at a 9.16x trailing 12-month Enterprise Value to Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation and Amortization (EV/EBITDA), which is a premium compared with the broader industry average of 5.89x. BP plcBP and ChevronCVX are trading at 2.93x and 8.04x, respectively. Given that the integrated energy giant is trading at a premium, what should investors do now? Before getting into it, let’s delve into the company’s fundamentals and overall business environment. West Texas Intermediate (“WTI”) crude is trading at more than the $95-per-barrel mark. The high prices are being driven by intensifying conflicts in the Middle East. The U.S. Energy Information Administration (“EIA”) in its latest short-term energy outlook projected WTI at $84.65 per barrel this year, higher than $65.40 last year. A highly favorable oil pricing environment is likely to continue supporting ExxonMobil’s exploration and production activities, similar to BP and Chevron. Importantly, upstream operations generate the majority of earnings for XOM. The company has a massive footprint in the Permian, the most prolific oil and gas play in the United States, and offshore Guyana. In the Permian, the integrated giant has been employing new drilling techniques and artificial intelligence to boost and optimize production volumes at lower cost structures. In Guyana, XOM has made several oil and gas discoveries, further highlighting its solid production outlook. Robust production from both assets has been aiding its top and bottom lines. In both resources, the breakeven costs are low. Investors should also keep in mind that XOM has a strong balance sheet that can support it during an unfavorable business environment. The debt-to-capitalization of ExxonMobil is 13.73%, significantly lower than 28.51% of the industry’s composite stocks. Coming to the integrated energy giant’s dividend commitment story, over the past 43 years, ExxonMobil has been rewarding shareholders with annual dividend hikes at an average rate of 5.8%. The positive developments are reflected in the price chart. In the past year, XOM has jumped 46%, outpacing the industry’s 45.1% growth. BP and CVX, two other integrated players in the same space, have gained 31.4% and 35.5%, respectively. Despite all the positive developments and elevated crude prices, it might not be the ideal time for investors to bet on ExxonMobil, as its valuation appears pricey. The company has operated in the country since 1923 and now holds interests in three joint ventures that have already raised output 15 percent year to date. The new agreements add acreage and improve fiscal terms, giving Chevron a platform for low-cost growth inside its existing portfolio. Under the agreements, Petroindependencia, S.A., in which a Chevron subsidiary holds a 49 percent interest, received rights to develop the adjacent Carabobo 1 and Carabobo-2-South-A areas. Chevron Corp. (CVX:NYSE; CVX:TSX) announced agreements with Venezuela establishing updated terms for its joint ventures in the country, including provisions covering fiscal, commercial, and legal terms and the assignment of additional acreage in the Orinoco Belt. The agreements support joint venture plans to invest more than US$7 billion over the next five years and more than double production to approximately 600,000 barrels per day compared with 2026. Chevron said total costs are less than US$20 per barrel. "Chevron's history in Venezuela spans more than a century, and our expanded position reflects our confidence in the country's deep resource potential and its ability to compete for investment within our portfolio for decades," Chevron Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Mike Wirth said. "With improved terms and additional acreage, we are strengthening a portfolio that we believe can deliver attractive low-cost oil growth, support energy supply, and create differentiated long-term value. This progress reflects the dedication of our Venezuelan employees and our long-standing focus on the responsible development of the country's resources." Under the agreements, Petroindependencia, S.A., in which a Chevron subsidiary holds a 49% interest, was assigned rights to develop the adjacent Carabobo 1 and Carabobo-2-South-A areas in Venezuela's Orinoco Belt. The greenfield sites expand the joint venture's existing operational footprint, where extra-heavy oil production is increasing. The agreements follow an April agreement under which Chevron increased its working interest in Petroindependencia to 49%, while its Petropiar, S.A. joint venture was assigned the rights to develop the adjacent Ayacucho 8 area. Chevron said its three Venezuelan joint ventures collectively increased production by 15% year-to-date. "We appreciate the leadership of the Administration, particularly the U.S. Department of Energy, and Secretary Wright's partnership in helping facilitate the conditions for further investment and growth," Wirth said. "Continued engagement between government and industry is essential to advancing projects that support energy security, economic growth, and continued investment." Chevron's presence in Venezuela dates to 1923. Its Petroindependencia and Petropiar, S.A. joint ventures operate extra-heavy oil projects in the Orinoco Oil Belt, while Petroboscan, S.A. is located in Zulia State in western Venezuela. Bloomberg reported on September 7 that Brent crude had approached US$100 per barrel after Saudi Arabia said attacks had halted operations at several energy facilities in the country's south. The publication said the global benchmark had been "less than US$1 away from triple figures" after rising the previous week amid renewed Middle East hostilities and increased buying from China, the world's largest oil importer. Oilprice.com reported early on September 8 that attacks on several Saudi energy facilities had caused fires, injuries, and temporary shutdowns. Saudi authorities said, "Several energy sector facilities and installations in the southern region of the Kingdom were targeted this morning." According to the report, specialized teams had begun containing the fires, securing the affected sites, and assessing damage, while authorities took measures intended to maintain operational continuity. Oilprice.com also reported that the latest disruptions had added to existing supply concerns in the Middle East, where shipping and energy flows had already faced pressure. A 400,000-barrel-per-day refinery on Saudi Arabia's Red Sea coast had been targeted multiple times since July, while more oil had been moved west to avoid the Strait of Hormuz. During Asian trading on September 8, Brent crude had reached US$98.70 per barrel, and West Texas Intermediate had reached US$94.12 per barrel. Later on September 8, TheStreet reported that physical oil flows had become an increasingly important influence on the market even as OPEC+ continued setting production quotas. The Strait of Hormuz, which had carried close to one-fifth of global crude and liquefied natural gas before fighting began on February 28, had effectively remained closed, with vessel traffic falling to a handful per day from more than 100 before the conflict. According to TheStreet, Jorge Leon of Rystad Energy said OPEC+ "currently has very limited power over the physical oil market." TheStreet also reported that seven OPEC+ members had left October production targets unchanged after raising output for six consecutive months. The report noted that production targets depended on barrels being able to reach ships and refineries, making transportation constraints an important factor in the physical market. It also cited GasBuddy petroleum analyst Patrick De Haan, who said diesel powered the "three t's" of the American economy, "trains, tractors, and trucks," underscoring the broader importance of crude and refined-product availability to transportation and freight. According to MarketBeat, Chevron Corp. had a "Moderate Buy" consensus rating based on 26 Wall Street analysts covering the stock over the previous 12 months. Of those analysts, 20 rated Chevron a Buy, five assigned Hold ratings, and one rated the stock a Sell. The consensus 12-month price target was US$211.35, with individual targets ranging from US$160 to US$243. Several analysts had recently raised their price targets. On September 3, BMO Capital Markets analyst Phillip Jungwirth maintained an Outperform rating and increased his target to US$235 from US$210. Piper Sandler analyst John Royall maintained an Overweight rating and raised his target to US$243 from US$207, while Wells Fargo analyst Sam Margolin maintained an Overweight rating and increased his target to US$230 from US$226. Those actions followed additional revisions in August. Morgan Stanley analyst Devin McDermott maintained an Overweight rating and raised his target to US$218 from US$210 on August 19. DBS Bank upgraded the stock to Moderate Buy on August 6. TD Cowen analyst Jason Gabelman maintained a Hold rating while increasing his price target to US$205 from US$200 on August 5. MarketBeat's historical comparison showed a shift in the analyst mix over the prior year. The current tally of 20 Buy, five Hold, and one Sell compares with 11 Buy, five Hold, and three Sell ratings one year earlier. Over the same comparison periods, the consensus rating moved from Hold to Moderate Buy, while the consensus price target increased from US$164.94 to US$211.35. Chevron's August 2026 investor presentation outlined capital expenditure guidance of US$18 billion to US$21 billion per year through 2030, along with affiliate capital expenditure guidance of US$1 billion to US$2 billion from 2026 through 2030. The presentation also listed production guidance of 2% to 3% compound annual growth and an approximately 10% average improvement in upstream cash margin. In the Permian, Chevron outlined a long-term production plateau with an option to grow and approximately US$5 billion in annual free cash flow through 2030. The presentation identified more than 3,100 net inventory locations with PV-10 breakevens below US$50 per barrel and more than 2,300 locations in the US$50 to US$70 range through 2040. Chevron also said new-well advanced chemical treatments were being scaled to 100% of company-operated Permian wells, while treatments were being piloted across its broader shale and tight portfolio. Across the DJ Basin, Bakken, and Argentina, the presentation projected a combined annual free cash flow of approximately US$2 billion through 2035. Chevron projected production in Argentina to grow by more than three times by 2035, with the Argentina portfolio described as approximately 75% oil weighted. The DJ Basin was listed with approximately 75% of inventory below a US$50 per barrel breakeven. In Guyana, the presentation identified more than 30 major discoveries and more than 11 billion barrels of oil equivalent of gross resource. Uaru was listed in execution with a start-up scheduled for 2026, Whiptail was in execution with a start-up scheduled for 2027, and Hammerhead was in execution with a start-up scheduled for 2029. Longtail was in front-end engineering design, with a final investment decision targeted for 2026. Chevron also stated that free cash flow growth from Guyana was expected beyond 2030. In the Eastern Mediterranean, Chevron reported that the Tamar Optimization Project and Leviathan additional capacity project had achieved first gas, Leviathan expansion had reached a final investment decision, and Aphrodite had entered front-end engineering design. The presentation listed full capacity for both the Leviathan Gathering Line and the Tamar Optimization Project in 2026. Leviathan Expansion Stage 1 was in execution with start-up scheduled for the end of the decade, while Aphrodite was in front-end engineering design with a final investment decision scheduled for 2027. Chevron also outlined continued activity in the Gulf of America, where it held approximately 1.7 million net acres and planned 10 to 15 exploration wells through 2030. Jack/St. Malo Stage 5 was listed as online, while Ballymore Stage 2 was in pre-front-end engineering design with a final investment decision scheduled for 2027. In Australia, the Jansz-Io Compression project was in execution with a start-up scheduled for 2028, while Gorgon Stage 3 was in execution with a start-up scheduled for the end of the decade. Chevron's Australian portfolio was also described as containing more than 40 trillion cubic feet of gross natural gas resource, with low-cost backfill projects and a projected average annual free cash flow of US$4 billion to US$5 billion. West African activity included the Aseng Gas Development in Equatorial Guinea, which had reached a final investment decision and was scheduled for start-up in 2028. YoYo Yolanda, spanning Equatorial Guinea and Cameroon, was in pre-front-end engineering design with a final investment decision scheduled for 2027. Nigeria's OML 89 Obokun project was also in pre-front-end engineering design with a final investment decision scheduled for 2027. Chevron said a 31-well Nigeria joint venture infill drilling program was underway, and 15 exploration and appraisal wells were planned over three years. An exploration well in Namibia was planned for 2026, while Chevron had entered two blocks in Guinea-Bissau. In chemicals, Chevron said its U.S. Gulf Coast and Qatar projects were more than 95% complete, with start-up anticipated in 2027. The major-project schedule identified the Ras Laffan Petrochemical Project in Qatar and the Golden Triangle Polymers Project in the United States as being in execution, with a start-up scheduled for 2027. title: CVX Testing Key Resistance: Stock Gains 1.91% (September 10, 2026) - JournalArta

On September 10, 2026: price 213.81 USD, trend uptrend, RSI 69.4, support 196.60, resistance 213.81. technical analysis of cvx stock. CVX Testing Key… Chevron Corp. shares on the NYSE rose to 213.81 USD on 9 September 2026, adding 1.91% on the day and extending a 1-month gain of 8.72%, according to Yahoo Finance data. The move matters because it places the stock right at the top of its recent trading range, with price now pressing against the upper Bollinger band and the 3-month high, a setup that often signals either a breakout attempt or a pause as momentum traders take profits. The broader structure remains constructive. Chevron is trading above both its SMA20 at 204.84 and SMA50 at 192.83, which means the short-term trend is above the medium-term trend and the market is still rewarding buyers. The SMA20 slope of 2.54% over 5 days shows the nearer-term average is still rising, a sign that the recent advance is not just a one-day spike but part of an active uptrend. There is no fresh MA-cross, so the chart is not flashing a new trend regime; instead, it is showing an established uptrend that is being tested near resistance. The key detail is where the price sits inside the range: the stock is at 100% of the 20-hour range, with 213.81 also matching the listed resistance, while the 3-month high stands at 215.28. That means Chevron is trading in the narrow zone where upside continuation becomes harder to prove without fresh demand.
That is the market’s test. Momentum is still positive, but it is no longer cleanly aligned. The MACD at 5.019 sits above its signal line at 4.663, and the positive histogram of 0.356 shows buyers still have the upper hand in trend terms. In plain English, MACD says the recent rise is still supported by underlying momentum rather than being a purely mechanical bounce. At the same time, the oscillator picture is getting stretched. The RSI at 69.4 is technically still in neutral territory, but it is close enough to the usual overbought threshold to suggest the stock is nearing a point where enthusiasm can cool. More importantly, the Stochastic %K at 91.6 and %D at 79.7 are both in overbought territory, which means the latest price is closing near the top of its recent range and has likely outrun short-term balance. That does not automatically mean reversal; it means the stock is more vulnerable to a stall if fresh buyers do not keep showing up. In other words, trend support is still there, but the short-term rubber band is stretched. The Bollinger Band structure adds an important layer to the story. Chevron is sitting at %B of 96%, which means the price is near the top of the band envelope and very close to the upper boundary at 214.67. When a stock rides that high inside its band, it often reflects strong demand — but it also warns that much of the easy upside for the moment may already be reflected in price. The 9.6% band width is described as normal, so this is not a volatility squeeze waiting to explode; it is a regular-volatility advance that has moved to an elevated position. ATR reinforces that interpretation. The ATR(14) of 3.88, equal to 1.8% of price, points to moderate day-to-day movement rather than a disorderly swing regime. That matters because moderate volatility near resistance often produces a slower, more tactical battle between continuation and consolidation. Volume is supportive but not dramatic. The latest print of 8,384,700 shares is only about 1.1× the 20-day average of 7,611,555, which means the advance is being confirmed by participation, but not by a surge of urgency. The rising OBV — on-balance volume, a measure that tracks whether volume tends to accumulate on up days — suggests money flow is still leaning positive. Yet the absence of a volume blowout near resistance argues for caution: this is confirmation, not capitulation from sellers. The market is now focused on a very tight band. Immediate support comes from the 20-hour support at 196.60, while the first technical ceiling is the current 213.81 resistance zone, followed by the upper Bollinger band at 214.67 and then the 3-month high at 215.28. Because the price is already at the top of the range, the next move matters more than the current level. If Chevron can hold above the 204.84 SMA20 after any cooling-off phase, the trend remains intact and the chart would look more like consolidation than reversal. If it fails to stay above the current band top and slips back through the mid-band area around 204.84, that would suggest the rally is pausing rather than extending. A break below 196.60 would be more meaningful, because it would put the stock back into the lower half of its recent range and challenge the idea that buyers remain in control. HOLD (wait & see) fits the current setup best because Chevron is in an uptrend, but it is also pressing against resistance with Stochastic overbought and %B at 96%, which raises the odds of near-term hesitation. The MACD remains positive, so the trend is not broken, and the price above SMA20 and SMA50 keeps the larger structure constructive. Still, the stock is already at the top of its recent range, so the next move needs confirmation rather than assumption. - Ideal Entry Range: 204.84 to 196.60, where price would be closer to the SMA20 and support
- Exit Target: 214.67 to 215.28, using the upper Bollinger band and 3-month high as the next technical ceiling
- Stop Loss protection: below 196.60, the listed 20-hour support This means Chevron is still trending higher, but it is now close enough to resistance that the chart is asking for proof before the move can extend further. Chevron’s next technical test is whether it can stay above 213.81 and challenge the 215.28 3-month high, with the market watching whether the latest volume and OBV support a clean break or a short pause. Broadcom Inc.’s AI chip business is showing little sign of slowing down, with the semiconductor giant expecting revenue from its AI chips to double in each of the next two years as demand from customers including Anthropic and OpenAI accelerates. The Palo Alto, California-based company expects AI semiconductor revenue to reach about $115 billion in fiscal 2027, up from roughly $58 billion expected in 2026, CEO Hock Tan said on the company’s third-quarter earnings call. The company sees another doubling to $230 billion in fiscal 2028, underscoring the strength of its custom AI accelerator and networking chip business. “In 2027, we have secured the supply to again double AI revenue to approximately $115 billion. Our demand actually exceeds this outlook, and we will work to improve supply,” Tan said. “In 2028… we have line of sight for fiscal 2028 AI semiconductor revenue growth to again double to $230 billion. Here again, we have secured the supply to meet this outlook.” Despite the strong outlook, Broadcom’s fourth-quarter revenue forecast, which implies 93% growth, came in below Wall Street’s expectations, sending AVGO shares 1.3% lower in overnight trading late Wednesday. The comments highlight how Broadcom has emerged as one of the biggest beneficiaries of the AI infrastructure boom beyond Nvidia. Its custom accelerators, or XPUs, are increasingly being adopted by major AI companies looking to build their own chips. AI chip sales more than tripled to $16.7 billion in the third quarter, lifting Broadcom's total revenue 86% to $29.59 billion, beating estimates of $29.36 billion. Adjusted profit came in at $3.32 ​per share, compared with estimates of $3.24. Anthropic is expected to become Broadcom’s largest XPU customer next year, with the AI startup planning to deploy another 5 gigawatts of Broadcom-designed TPU v8i chips in 2027 and an additional 10 gigawatts in 2028. OpenAI is also expected to become a major customer, with Broadcom seeing a path for the ChatGPT maker to deploy more than 5 gigawatts of its next-generation Jalapeno XPU in 2028. “These two guys, Anthropic and OpenAI, I mean, these are… it’s like you have two geniuses in the middle of outer Mongolia. They need to go to college to fulfill their potential,” Tan said, suggesting that while both companies have enormous potential, they need access to Broadcom’s chips and infrastructure (“college”) to fully realize it. “We do what we can to help them, and part of it is creating sources of financing to help these companies with the leading-edge frontier models in the world be able to play in the same playing field and be able to offer these great technology products to the world,” he added. Broadcom has secured supplies for wafers, substrates and memory needed to meet its 2027 and 2028 AI revenue targets. The company also plans to begin deploying its Singapore substrate facility in fiscal 2027 to ease a key supply bottleneck. Moor Insights & Strategy CEO and analyst Patrick Moorhead said Broadcom delivered a “strong, but not flawless” third quarter, arguing that the key takeaway was its AI execution rather than the modest revenue beat. He pointed to Broadcom’s $16.7 billion in Q3 AI revenue and $21.7 billion Q4 outlook as evidence that the company is successfully converting its AI backlog into sales. Moorhead also highlighted Broadcom’s broader AI infrastructure advantage, spanning custom XPU co-design, Ethernet switching, SerDes, optics, packaging and foundry access, but cautioned that the results “do not prove broad NVIDIA displacement.” “The wrinkle is software, and the release does not resolve customer concentration, Google multisourcing, bookings conversion, AI networking mix, first-generation XPU yields or the fiscal 2027 AI bridge,” he said. Future Fund Managing Director Gary Black noted the improvement in AVGO stock after-hours “as investors responded favorably to the company’s AI rev growth guidance”. “As the AI Rev strength becomes clearer to investors, I expect the stock to recover somewhat,” he said. title: Why BP Is One of the Best Oil Stocks to Buy Right Now - The Globe and Mail
content: With oil prices surging again, BP BP) is emerging as one of the more compelling large-cap energy stocks to consider. Brent crude climbed back above $100 per barrel on Wednesday, creating another powerful cash-flow tailwind for integrated oil producers. That is particularly attractive for BP, considering the company was already generating immense amounts of cash before crude's latest move higher. Along with strengthening fundamentals and an improving earnings outlook, investors are getting a dividend yield of more than 4.5% and a stock that still trades at a very reasonable valuation. Last month, BP's second-quarter results showcased just how much cash the company can generate in a favorable energy environment. Operating cash flow surged 73% year over year to $10.86 billion in Q2, compared with $6.27 billion in the prior-year period. Underlying replacement cost profit more than doubled to $5.73 billion, aided by higher energy prices, stronger refining margins, and trading results. Importantly, this cash generation is strengthening BP's balance sheet as well. Net debt fell to $22.25 billion, compared with $26.04 billion a year earlier. At the end of Q2, BP had over $45 billion in cash and equivalents and more than $294 billion in total assets, which is nicely above its total liabilities of $218.2 billion. Investors are also being rewarded directly, with BP raising its quarterly dividend by more than 4% to $0.52 per share. With Brent now above $100, BP's already impressive cash-flow profile could receive another boost if elevated oil prices persist. BP still has several avenues to expand earnings and cash flow beyond simply relying on higher commodity prices. The company has been ramping up a wave of major upstream developments, with eight of 10 major projects scheduled between 2025 and 2027 already online as of July. BP has also targeted adjusted free-cash-flow growth of more than 20% annually from 2024 through 2027, along with return on average capital employed (ROACE) above 16% in 2027. Near-term earnings expectations are particularly strong. The Zacks Consensus currently calls for 2026 EPS of $6.45, representing growth of more than 123%, while revenue is projected to rise roughly 21% to $232.88 billion. Although FY27 EPS is projected to normalize to $4.95 following an exceptional FY26, earnings estimates have climbed sharply over the last 60 days, with the FY27 EPS consensus rising nearly 25% (F2 below) and FY26 EPS estimates jumping almost 30% (F1). Despite its rising earnings outlook and robust cash generation, BP stock remains relatively inexpensive even after a 30% year-to-date surge toward 52-week highs. Trading at around $45 a share, BP stock is at a 7X forward earnings multiple. This is still a notable discount to oil giants Chevron CVX) and Exxon Mobil XOM), which trade at roughly 12X forward earnings, respectively. BP's price-to-cash-flow ratio of 4X also sits well below many of its large-cap oil peers, with Chevron and Exxon both trading at around 12X cash flow. That combination of a low earnings multiple, massive cash flows, and a dividend yield above 4.5% makes BP particularly appealing for investors looking for both value and income exposure to elevated oil prices. Of course, a sharp reversal in crude prices would temper BP's earnings and cash-flow outlook. Still, the current setup is difficult to overlook, with Brent above $100, BP producing billions of dollars in quarterly cash flow, reducing debt, growing its dividend, and advancing several major upstream projects. At the moment, BP stock currently sports a Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy) and has an overall "A" VGM Zacks Style Scores grade for the combination of Value, Growth, and Momentum. For investors seeking exposure to high oil prices without paying a premium valuation, BP looks like one of the best stocks to consider right now. content: Shares of major oil stocks and index funds jumped in the overnight trading session headed into Monday after oil prices spiked on U.S. President Donald Trump’s comment that time was running out for Iran. American oil companies also got a sentiment boost after Trump said last week that China had agreed to buy crude oil from the U.S. following the recently-concluded bilateral summit in Beijing. Shares of the United States Oil Fund (USO) rose 2%, while Exxon Mobil Corp. (XOM) climbed 0.7%, Conoco Phillips (COP) gained 0.9%, Chevron Corp. (CVX) was up 0.45%, and Venture Global Inc. (VG) was up more than 1% at the time of writing. Oil prices surged after Trump said in a post on Truth Social on Sunday, "For Iran, the Clock is Ticking, and they better get moving, FAST, or there won't be anything left of them. TIME IS OF THE ESSENCE!" The comments come shortly after the president’s visit to China, a country with close ties to Tehran. Investors were hoping for a significant breakthrough after the visit. Brent crude futures expiring in July were up about 1.81%, trading at around $111.30 a barrel, while WTI crude futures expiring in June were 2.18% higher, at $107.72 a barrel at the time of writing. The conflict between the U.S. and Iran has stayed high despite a ceasefire announced in early April. The U.S. has continued to blockade Iranian ports, even as the critical Strait of Hormuz has stayed shut since the conflict began. Meanwhile, reports have said that Iran has called the U.S. blockade an “act of war,” threatening further damage to countries around the world if the blockade continued. Mohsen Rezaei, a member of Tehran’s Expediency Council and former IRGC commander, has reportedly said that the Iranian military is ready for further confrontation. “We advise the US military to end the siege before the Sea of Oman becomes your graveyard,” Rezaei reportedly said. “It is America that must prove itself now,” he said. “Our armed forces have their finger on the trigger, and, at the same time, diplomacy continues.” Meanwhile, China agreed to buy crude oil from the U.S. last week. “They have an insatiable appetite for energy, and we have unlimited energy,” Trump said in an interview with Fox News, adding that “we’re doing twice as much oil and gas, as they are,” referring to the U.S. producing more oil and gas than Saudi Arabia and Russia combined. Oil and gas supermajor Chevron CVX is benefiting from strong production and Hess buyout synergies. Structural cost reductions have also improved the economics of its massive energy portfolio. But for investors, the big question is whether Chevron is turning that operating strength into consistently attractive returns. Looking at return on invested capital (ROIC), cash conversion and earnings linearity, we can say that the company is generating plenty of cash, but its returns and earnings consistency leave room for improvement. In the last reported quarter, Chevron's worldwide production jumped 20% year over year to a record 4.07 million barrels of oil equivalent per day, powered by the Hess acquisition, Permian growth, and the Gulf of America. On the cost side, Chevron hit $3 billion in annual run-rate structural savings and $1.5 billion in Hess synergies— both six months ahead of schedule. Management is also guiding toward spending 25% less capital per barrel of oil equivalent in 2026 than in 2025. Put together, Chevron is pumping more oil, spending less to do it, and cutting the capital it needs per barrel going forward. Based on our proprietary calculation, Chevron's trailing-12-month ROIC stands at 7.8%, above its own 10-year median of 6.3%, indicating that capital efficiency remains better than its longer-term historical norm. But the more recent trend is less encouraging. CVX's ROIC has slipped from a 5-year median of 9.4% to a 3-year median of 8.3% and now stands at 7.8%. At the same time, its current ROIC is below the 8.6% industry median. Close peers like ExxonMobil XOM and Shell SHEL also generate higher ROIC, at 9.2% and 10.2%, respectively. The production growth and cost discipline are happening, but they haven't yet translated into a sustained improvement in capital efficiency. Part of the disconnect may be the industry's commodity sensitivity. Higher production and lower unit costs can improve the underlying economics, but weaker oil and gas prices can still compress profits and ROIC faster than the capital base adjusts. If Hess synergies, structural cost cuts, and a lighter capital footprint in U.S. shale keep compounding, ROIC can increase from here. A downturn in commodity prices or slippage on execution could just as easily pull it the other way. The next few quarters of ROIC data will matter more than any single production headline. If ROIC shows how productively Chevron uses its capital, cash flow conversion shows whether those earnings are turning into real money. And here, the picture is much cleaner. Chevron's TTM cash-flow conversion runs at 220.1%, with free-cash-flow conversion at 131.2%, per our proprietary calculations. Both are a bit below their historical medians, but still comfortably strong. In the last reported quarter, Chevron generated $19.7 billion of operating cash flow excluding working capital, $15.4 billion of adjusted free cash flow, and a record $8.4 billion debt paydown. Chevron is effective at converting profits into cash to reduce debt, fund investments and return capital to shareholders. That helps offset the ROIC concern. Even if capital efficiency is middling now, the balance sheet is getting materially stronger. Chevron's earnings also lack consistency. Per our proprietary model, its 10-year EPS linearity is only 30.9%, below the 34.8% industry median and far below the 100% ideal baseline. Meanwhile, 10-year EPS CAGR (on a TTM basis) of 9.5% trails the industry median of 13.2%. That inconsistency largely comes down to commodity exposure. Chevron's earnings move with oil, gas and refining prices rather than following a steady operational trajectory. Mixed downstream demand and softer energy prices can therefore add further volatility to earnings. Peers show a similar spread. ExxonMobil's EPS linearity sits at 37.5%, while Shell's at 29.1%, suggesting earnings volatility is a sector-wide feature. Chevron's higher production, cost cuts and Hess synergies are improving the business, and the benefits are already showing up in strong cash generation. But the improvement in operations has not yet translated into a similar improvement in ROIC as Chevron's earnings remain tied to the highly cyclical energy market. Shares of Chevron have gained 38% year to date, outperforming the industry, ExxonMobil and Shell. From a valuation perspective— in terms of forward price-to-earnings ratio— Chevron is trading at a premium compared with the industry average. The stock is also trading above its five-year mean of 11.81. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for CVX's 2026 earnings is pegged at $16.51 per share, indicating 126% year-over-year growth. The company's "low" balance sheet makes room for steady capital allocation execution through the market cycle, the analyst reportedly said, but added that it believes Exxon is trading near fair value multiples on 2027 estimates. title: CVX Stock Has A New Bull Case — Why Bank Of America Favors Chevron Over Exxon As Hormuz Risks Push Oil Prices Higher - Stocktwits
content: Chevron Corp. (CVX) could benefit if tensions between Iran and the U.S. remain elevated and the Strait of Hormuz closes again, according to Bank of America. The bank has a ‘Buy’ rating on the oil and gas company and a $210 price target on the shares, implying around 19% upside from Wednesday’s close. CVX stock was down nearly 1% at the time of writing on Thursday. “CVX is our preferred way to play [increased oil prices] … integrateds are pricing in <$70/bbl LT Brent, which we see as a particularly attractive entry point,” Bank Of America (BofA) said in a note to clients, according to a report in CNBC. “We prefer CVX to XOM given its Venezuela presence, lack of Middle East exposure, and higher earnings torque to the shifts upward in prices in 2026/27,” the firm added. The Iran war has pushed crude prices higher amid concerns over supply disruptions, with control of the Strait of Hormuz at the center of the conflict. The waterway handles around 20% of global oil shipments, making any disruption a major risk for energy markets. However, oil futures dipped slightly on Thursday. At the time of writing, International Brent crude futures (Co1) were down 2.56% at $76 per barrel, while West Texas Intermediate futures (CL1) fell 2.3% to $71.83 a barrel. Despite Thursday’s slight dip, Bank of America expects oil prices to remain elevated as the U.S. continues its campaign against Iran and brushes off efforts to reach a settlement. “Medium term restocking demand should support a $70/bbl level, assuming that the strait reopening is not essentially flawless from here, which seems like a safe assumption (at least as of today),” the BofA analyst wrote. The analyst added that while a large amount of crude has been announced as potentially coming out of the Middle East in the near future, the delivery of those shipments depends largely on Iran tensions easing, “which looks less likely.” On Stocktwits, retail sentiment for CVX was ‘bullish,’ unchanged over the past 24 hours, while message volume was ‘normal’ at the time of writing. Bank of America’s rating aligns with broader Wall Street sentiment. According to Koyfin data, 19 of the 24 analysts covering Chevron have a ‘Buy’ or ‘Strong Buy’ rating on the stock. The 12-month average price target stands at $216.48, implying potential upside of about 23% from the last close. The CVX stock has gained around 15.5% year to date. Small-cap stocks seem to be having their day in the sun, with their best first-half performance since 1991, as per Charlie Bilello, Chief Market Strategist at Creative Planning. In a post on X, the analyst said that U.S. small caps had gained more than 22% in the first half of 2026, “their best first half performance since 1991.” “Their outperformance vs. Large Caps of over 12% was the widest for a first half since 2001,” he added. This is indeed true – the Russell 2000 index, which tracks the performance of about 2,000 of the smallest publicly traded companies in the U.S., has far outperformed benchmark indexes, including the S&P 500, Dow Jones, and Nasdaq, in the first half of 2026. According to data from Koyfin, the Russell 2000 gained nearly 22%, while the S&P 500 and Dow Jones gained about 9% each, and the Nasdaq rose about 13%. All 11 sectors in the Russell 2000 ended the first half of the year in positive territory, according to Franklin Templeton. Technology was the biggest contributor, the investment management firm said, followed by industrials, financials and healthcare, while semiconductors, electrical equipment, banks and electronic equipment were among the top-performing industries. The trend seems to have been strong, especially in the second quarter of 2026, with small and micro-cap stocks leading the way. “In the bullish second quarter of 2026, small- and micro-cap stocks continued to lead the US equity markets in a robust period for equities of all sizes and styles,” Franklin Templeton said earlier this week. “Resilience amid mixed signals was once again the main theme, as geopolitical tensions remained unresolved, inflation lingered, and energy prices were still volatile, depending on the changing state of the war with Iran on any given day,” it added. The iShares Russell 2000 ETF (IWM) was also trading higher, although sentiment was ‘bearish’ at the time of writing. As per Franklin Templeton, the trend is likely to continue through the year, even though “small-cap market leadership is scarcely 15 months old.” The firm said that its research found that the sensitivity of small-cap performance to interest rate changes is not as closely correlated as is often assumed, as “it also tends to discount (if not ignore) the performance of small-cap companies with little or no debt.” As per the firm, the most important point to consider is that the combination of small-cap valuations and earnings “should be more than sufficient to keep the asset class in the leadership role.” Morningstar Wealth chief multi-asset strategist Dominic Pappalardo also holds a similar belief. “The quiet surge in small caps has momentum to continue,” Pappalardo said, as per a report on the website from Wednesday. The firm noted that U.S. small-cap equities have underperformed their large- and mid-cap peers over the past 15 years. Pappalardo believes the group is more diversified than large caps: “40% of the S&P 500 is made up of the top 10 names, and nine of those are tech or tech-related,” he said. At the same time, the 10 largest small caps account for a much smaller percentage of the small-cap indexes. Meanwhile, the top 10 constituents make up a much smaller share of small-cap indexes. Moreover, on a relative basis, small-cap stocks appear to be more undervalued now than they have in a long time, the report noted, adding that the Wealth team believes large caps look overvalued. On September 9, 2026: price 209.80 USD, trend uptrend, RSI 65.2, support 196.60, resistance 211.78. technical analysis of cvx stock. CVX Stock Gains — full… Chevron’s shares on the NYSE rose to 209.80 USD as of 8 September 2026 at 20:30 WIB, up 0.58% on the day and 7.64% over the past month, according to Yahoo Finance data. The move leaves CVX above its SMA20 at 203.99 and well above its SMA50 at 191.93, a setup that says the stock is not merely bouncing but remains in a broader upward structure. With price sitting near the top of its recent band and momentum still positive, the chart is signaling strength — but also that the easy part of the rally may already be behind it. The key message from the price structure is that Chevron is still trading in an established uptrend. The stock is above both its short-term and medium-term moving averages, and the SMA20 slope of 2.64% over 5 days shows the near-term trend is still rising rather than flattening out. That matters because a rising SMA20 often acts like a moving floor: when price stays above it, dips tend to be bought faster than they are in a weak tape. The share price is also positioned near the upper end of its recent range, with 209.80 USD sitting at about 87% of the 20-hour range between 196.60 support and 211.78 resistance. That placement suggests buyers have already pushed the stock close to a known ceiling. The 3-month high of 213.31 is only slightly above current levels, so the market is testing a zone where supply has previously appeared. What this means in plain language: Chevron is strong, but it is now close to where strength has to prove itself again. The momentum picture is constructive, though not explosive. RSI at 65.2 is still described as neutral in this dataset, but it sits high enough to show the stock has been in sustained demand. RSI measures the speed of recent gains versus losses; readings that climb toward the upper end of the range usually mean buyers are in control, while also warning that upside can become more stretched if the reading pushes much higher. The stochastic oscillator, at %K 77.3 and %D 78.4, is also marked neutral, but the pair is hovering near the upper band of its range. Stochastic is useful for spotting whether price is closing near the top or bottom of its recent trading window. Here, it says Chevron is still trading near the high end of that window, which supports the uptrend but also signals that the stock is no longer cheap in short-term momentum terms. The cleaner confirmation comes from MACD. With MACD at 4.816 above its signal line at 4.611 and a positive histogram of 0.205, momentum remains on the bullish side. MACD is a trend-following tool, and when the main line stays above the signal line, it usually implies the trend still has internal support. The histogram being positive means that bullish momentum is still expanding, even if only modestly. In other words, the chart is not flashing reversal — it is saying the uptrend still has fuel, just not unlimited fuel. Volatility is present, but not excessive. Chevron’s ATR(14) of 3.74, equal to 1.8% of price, points to a market that can move meaningfully without being disorderly. ATR, or average true range, is a measure of typical daily movement; in this case it suggests traders should expect normal-sized swings rather than a sharp volatility break. Bollinger Bands add an important nuance. Price is trading near the upper band at 213.52, with the middle band at 203.99 and the lower band at 194.45. The %B reading of 80% means the stock is leaning toward the top of the band structure, which usually reflects strength. At the same time, the 9.3% band width is described as normal, so this is not a squeeze setup — not the kind of compressed chart that often precedes a sharp breakout. Instead, it looks like an orderly trend with room to continue, but without a volatility trigger forcing a decisive move. Volume is broadly supportive. Last volume came in at 7,703,900, just above the 7,494,810 average, or about 1.0× normal. That matters because price moves are more convincing when they are backed by participation. The rising OBV, or on-balance volume, reinforces the idea that money flow has been net positive: more volume has been associated with up days than down days. The immediate battleground is clear. Resistance at 211.78 is the first level the market must overcome, while the 3-month high at 213.31 is the next reference point above that. On the downside, support at 196.60 is the first important level that has to hold to keep the bullish structure intact. Below that, the SMA20 at 203.99 becomes the key trend marker; if price slips under it, the recent advance starts to lose some of its short-term momentum character. If Chevron clears 211.78 and holds above that area, the chart would be signaling that buyers are willing to pay up near the recent high. If it fails there, the stock may simply rotate back toward the middle of its Bollinger Band at 203.99, which would be a normal pause rather than a trend break. HOLD (wait & see) because the trend is still positive, but price is already pressing against near-term resistance and the upper Bollinger area. - MACD remains positive, with the main line above signal and a bullish histogram, which supports trend continuation.

- %B at 80% and price near 211.78 resistance suggest the stock is extended enough that fresh upside needs confirmation, not assumption. - Exit target: 211.78 to 213.31
- Stop loss protection: below 196.60 Plain English: Chevron still looks strong, but the chart is asking for proof before the next leg higher. Global benchmark crude has moved higher in recent sessions as the confrontation between the United States and Iran continues to unsettle shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Strikes and counter-strikes attributed to both sides have prompted several tanker operators to reroute or pause transits through the waterway, feeding a structural premium into benchmark pricing that has held up for weeks rather than fading within a single session. For a diversified major such as Chevron, a firmer crude tape tends to support upstream cash generation across its global production base, even as downstream refining margins face a more mixed picture when feedstock costs climb faster than product prices. Traders have also noted that freight availability through the strait has tightened further as insurers reassess coverage terms for vessels transiting the corridor, adding another layer of cost on top of the underlying crude price move. That combination of higher freight and higher benchmark pricing has been a recurring theme across the wider energy complex since the standoff between Washington and Tehran first escalated earlier in the year. Chevron operates across upstream exploration and production, downstream refining and marketing, and a growing chemicals and midstream footprint. The company's production base spans the Permian Basin, the Gulf of Mexico, Kazakhstan, Australia and a long-standing position in Venezuela that has recently returned to the center of corporate strategy. Chevron also maintains a sizable liquefied natural gas footprint through its Australian assets, giving it exposure to both crude and gas benchmarks. The company's scale and geographic diversification allow capital to be redirected toward whichever region offers the strongest near-term economics, a flexibility that has become especially relevant as Middle East tensions complicate planning for peers with more concentrated regional exposure. Chevron's downstream network, spanning refining, marketing and lubricants operations across several continents, further broadens the company's revenue base beyond pure upstream production, giving it a somewhat different overall profile than smaller independent producers that lack any downstream counterweight to swings in crude pricing. Chevron has confirmed plans to channel a multibillion-dollar sum through its Venezuelan joint ventures over the next several years, aiming to roughly double production from the South American country. The plan follows a period during which Chevron remained the only major U.S. oil company still operating in Venezuela, maintaining a foothold even through periods of sanctions-related uncertainty that sidelined other international operators. The scale of the commitment reflects renewed confidence in Venezuela's heavy crude reserves, among the largest in the world, and Chevron's long operating history in the country's Orinoco Belt, where the company has decades of technical experience managing extra-heavy crude production. Company commentary framed the Venezuela plan as a long-cycle growth pillar distinct from the shorter-cycle Permian program, noting that the extra-heavy crude produced in the Orinoco Belt typically requires specialized processing and blending capacity that Chevron has already built out over its long tenure operating in the country. The expansion follows updated agreements that grant Chevron improved fiscal, commercial and legal terms alongside additional acreage in the Orinoco Belt. Company disclosures indicate the three Venezuelan joint ventures will channel the capital through the balance of the decade, with total production costs expected to remain competitive relative to global heavy crude benchmarks. The revised terms are widely viewed as a meaningful shift from the arrangements that governed Chevron's Venezuela operations in prior years, providing a clearer path for the company to commit additional capital without the same degree of contractual uncertainty that characterized the prior period. Personnel familiar with the joint venture structure have noted that the added acreage sits adjacent to fields Chevron already operates, allowing existing processing infrastructure and pipeline connections to be leveraged rather than requiring an entirely new build-out, a factor that could help keep development timelines shorter than a greenfield project of similar scale. The Venezuela announcement arrived alongside broader diplomatic developments involving the United States government and Venezuela's oil sector, including a separate arrangement giving Washington an equity stake in a private oil firm operating in the country. Taken together, the developments point to a broader normalization of U.S. engagement with Venezuela's energy sector after years of restricted activity. For Chevron, the timing coincides with a period of firmer global crude pricing tied to the Iran-U.S. standoff, meaning any incremental barrels brought online in Venezuela would be sold into a market already supported by geopolitical tightness elsewhere. Diplomatic observers have cautioned that Venezuela's political landscape has historically proven difficult to predict over multi-year horizons, meaning the pace at which Chevron's expanded commitment translates into actual barrels will likely depend on continued stability in the surrounding commercial and legal framework. Across the broader energy sector, companies with exposure to Middle East production or shipping routes have been reassessing near-term planning in response to the Hormuz-related disruption. Some buyers of Middle East crude grades have reportedly sought alternative cargoes from the Atlantic Basin, a dynamic that could indirectly support demand for barrels produced outside the Middle East, including Chevron's growing Venezuela output. Freight brokers have also pointed to a broader reshuffling of tanker routes as owners weigh the added cost of transiting the strait against longer voyages around alternative corridors, a dynamic that has kept overall shipping capacity tighter than usual across the Atlantic Basin trade lanes that Chevron's non-Middle East barrels typically rely on. Chevron's downstream refining network continues to navigate the balance between higher feedstock costs tied to firmer crude and product pricing that has not always kept pace. The company's chemical operations, run through a joint venture structure, provide a partially offsetting revenue stream that is less directly correlated with crude price swings than the upstream segment, offering a measure of balance across the broader portfolio during periods of geopolitical volatility. Marketing and lubricants operations round out the downstream business, providing a further layer of diversification that has historically helped smooth quarter-to-quarter swings tied to refining margin volatility, particularly during periods when crude benchmarks move sharply on geopolitical headlines rather than underlying demand fundamentals. Beyond Venezuela, Chevron continues to lean on the Permian Basin as a core growth engine, alongside continued development in the Gulf of Mexico and its long-running position in Kazakhstan's Tengiz field. Each of these areas has delivered steady production gains in recent years, complementing the renewed push in Venezuela and reinforcing Chevron's position as one of the more geographically diversified integrated majors. The company's Australian liquefied natural gas assets add a further dimension to that diversification, giving Chevron exposure to gas benchmarks in addition to crude, a combination that has provided a measure of stability during periods when crude and gas prices move in different directions. The broader oil and gas sector continues to navigate a period defined by capital discipline, consolidation among mid-sized producers, and growing emphasis on steady production growth over aggressive expansion. Chevron's approach to Venezuela, built around improved contractual terms rather than speculative early-stage exploration, reflects that broader industry preference for lower-uncertainty growth options even in a firmer crude price environment. As a fully integrated major, Chevron's diversified footprint across upstream, downstream and chemicals continues to differentiate it from smaller independent producers with more concentrated regional exposure. That diversification, paired with the newly expanded Venezuela position, gives the company multiple avenues for production growth that do not depend solely on Middle East supply dynamics. Company commentary has repeatedly emphasized capital discipline as a guiding principle across the portfolio, meaning the Venezuela commitment is expected to be phased in alongside continued spending restraint elsewhere in the business rather than layered on top of an otherwise unchanged spending program. Despite the near-term tailwind tied to firmer crude, integrated majors continue to navigate a set of longer-running challenges, including the complexity of operating in jurisdictions with shifting regulatory and diplomatic conditions, rising costs tied to heavy crude processing, and the broader industry-wide push to diversify into lower-carbon energy sources. Chevron's Venezuela expansion illustrates how those challenges can coexist with meaningful long-cycle growth prospects when contractual terms improve. Labor and equipment availability across the global oilfield services sector has also tightened in recent quarters, a dynamic that could affect the pace at which Chevron and its peers are able to mobilize crews and materials for new development phases in Venezuela and elsewhere. Chevron continues to compete with a small group of similarly scaled integrated majors, several of which have historically avoided re-entering Venezuela given the country's complex regulatory history. That relative scarcity of competition in the country gives Chevron a distinctive position among its peer group, even as the broader competitive landscape across the Permian and Gulf of Mexico remains crowded with independent and integrated producers alike. Peers with more concentrated Middle East exposure face a different set of considerations than Chevron during the current standoff, since their production and shipping routes sit closer to the affected corridor, whereas Chevron's Venezuela and Permian barrels move through largely unaffected logistics networks. The renewed focus on Middle East supply routes and Chevron's simultaneous push into Venezuela together illustrate how integrated majors are navigating a period of both geopolitical uncertainty and long-cycle growth planning. Coverage of the broader integrated major group has also continued to note how downstream refining margins are responding to the current period of firmer crude feedstock costs, with Chevron's results expected to offer one of the clearer signals of how that dynamic is playing out across the wider sector heading into the next round of quarterly disclosures.
