Chevron Corporation CVX is strengthening its position in Venezuela, potentially creating another important production-growth opportunity for the integrated energy giant. The company recently announced expanded agreements covering its Venezuelan joint ventures, including additional acreage in the Orinoco Belt and improved fiscal, commercial and legal terms. The agreements support plans for more than $7 billion of investment over the next five years and are expected to more than double joint-venture production to approximately 600,000 barrels per day compared with 2026 levels. This move comes as Chevron is benefiting from strong operating performance, a stronger balance sheet and faster-than-expected Hess synergies. However, Venezuela also brings geopolitical and execution risks. Therefore, investors must determine whether the expansion provides enough upside to justify CVX's valuation. Chevron's Venezuela opportunity is significant because it already has an established operating platform in the country. Management said Chevron's three Venezuelan joint ventures increased production from approximately 40,000 barrels per day several years ago to 250,000 barrels and subsequently to 280,000 barrels, representing 15% growth in production from the three Venezuelan joint ventures over the past six months. Management expects production from the existing JVs to increase as much as 50% through the end of 2028. Chevron's long operating history in Venezuela is another advantage. Management said the company has been active in the country for 103 years and remains encouraged by its heavy-oil resources and additional opportunities. However, Chevron has emphasized that new investments must offer competitive terms and compete for capital with other projects across its global portfolio. The strategy could therefore add another layer of production growth without making Venezuela the sole driver of Chevron's investment case. Chevron has the financial strength to pursue additional opportunities while continuing to improve its balance sheet. In the second quarter, the company reported $12.1 billion in earnings, or $6.11 per share, while adjusted earnings reached $12 billion, or $6.06. Worldwide production increased 20% year over year to a record 4.07 million barrels of oil equivalent per day. Cash generation was also impressive. Operating cash flow reached $22.6 billion, while free cash flow totaled approximately $18.1 billion. Chevron reduced total debt by a record $8.4 billion, lowering its net debt-to-CFFO ratio to 0.6x. CVX is also benefiting from the Hess acquisition. The company achieved $1.5 billion in annual run-rate Hess synergies, six months ahead of schedule, while also achieving $3 billion in annual run-rate structural cost reductions six months ahead of schedule. These improvements provide Chevron with greater financial flexibility as it evaluates additional investments in Venezuela and elsewhere. Chevron's expansion is not occurring in isolation. Repsol REPYY and Eni E are also increasing their exposure to Venezuela, making them relevant peers for investors assessing the country's energy opportunity. Repsol owns 40% of Petroquiriquire, with PDVSA holding the remaining 60%. The company has been pursuing greater operational control and higher production from its Venezuelan assets. Repsol also has a 50% interest in the Cardón IV gas project alongside Eni and is assessing additional opportunities in the country. Eni also has significant Venezuelan exposure. The company owns 50% of Cardón IV alongside Repsol and has interests in other Venezuelan assets. Eni signed a 25-year contract, with a possible extension, under which it becomes the exclusive operator of the Junín-5 area in the Orinoco Belt. The field contains 35 billion barrels of certified oil in place and currently produces approximately 12,000 barrels per day. The activity of Chevron, Eni and Repsol suggests that Venezuela could represent a growing opportunity for international energy companies. However, all three companies remain exposed to political, regulatory and operational uncertainties. Despite Chevron's strong fundamentals, the stock has underperformed these two peers over the past year. CVX's shares have gained approximately 35.5%, compared with 54.6% for Eni and 90.3% for Repsol. The comparison shows that investors have rewarded Eni and Repsol more strongly. Their Venezuelan exposure is one factor supporting the comparison, although stock performance also reflects differences in portfolio composition, commodity exposure and valuation. Chevron's advantage is its much broader portfolio. Guyana, the Permian Basin, the Gulf of America and Hess assets provide additional sources of production and cash-flow growth. The valuation comparison is less favorable for CVX. Chevron currently trades at a forward P/E of approximately 13.68, compared with 10.08 for Eni and 7.16 for Repsol. Chevron's premium score can partly be justified by its scale, diversified asset portfolio, stronger balance sheet and production growth. However, investors are paying more for each dollar of expected earnings. Continued execution will therefore be essential for CVX to maintain this premium. Another positive factor is the improvement in earnings expectations. Over the past 60 days, the Zacks Consensus Estimate trend for CVX's EPS has increased 21.33% for 2026 and 6.12% for 2027. The upward revisions indicate improving analyst expectations for Chevron's earnings potential. Strong production growth, cost reductions and Hess synergies could continue to support results. Nevertheless, energy earnings remain sensitive to commodity prices and operating conditions. Venezuela remains the most important risk to the expansion. Changes in government policies, fiscal terms, sanctions, geopolitical conditions or operating restrictions could affect Chevron's ability to realize the expected returns. Commodity-price volatility is another concern. Chevron's strong second-quarter results benefited from higher commodity prices, increased production and stronger refining performance. A weaker oil-price environment could reduce the cash-flow benefits associated with additional Venezuelan production. Capital allocation is also important. Chevron has numerous competing growth opportunities, including Guyana, the Permian, Argentina and other international projects. Management has emphasized that Venezuela must compete for capital based on expected returns. Chevron's expanded Venezuelan JV strategy strengthens its long-term production story. The company's existing Venezuelan operations are already growing, while strong second-quarter cash generation, lower leverage and faster-than-expected Hess synergies provide a solid financial foundation. However, CVX has underperformed Eni and Repsol over the past year while trading at a higher forward P/E multiple. The geopolitical and execution risks surrounding Venezuela also make the investment case less straightforward. With a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold), the balanced view is to hold CVX rather than aggressively chase the stock. Existing shareholders have reasons to remain invested given Chevron's strong fundamentals and multiple growth opportunities. New investors, however, may want to wait for a more attractive valuation or clearer evidence that the expanded Venezuelan JVs can generate compelling shareholder returns. title: ExxonMobil's CEO Called Venezuela 'Uninvestable.' Trump Says It's Going In Anyway. Here's Why Investors Should Pay Attention. - The Globe and Mail
content: A lot has changed in Venezuela since ExxonMobil's CEO called it "uninvestable." Rival Chevron recently signed an enhanced agreement in Venezuela, supporting a significant expansion of its operations there. This past January, ExxonMobil's(NYSE: XOM) CEO Darren Woods called Venezuela "uninvestable" during a meeting at the White House, a remark that didn't sit well with President Trump. Fast forward a few months, and the President recently publicly announced that "Exxon is going in" to Venezuela. While ExxonMobil hasn't confirmed plans to reenter the country following its exit two decades ago, much has changed since the year began. Here's why investors should pay attention to the President's assertion that ExxonMobil is returning to Venezuela. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again.In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » At a recent press event unveiling a massive U.S. oil deal with Venezuela, President Trump highlighted that Exxon and Chevron(NYSE: CVX) are among the many big oil companies heading into Venezuela. Chevron has already confirmed its expansion in the country, noting that its two decades of patience have finally paid off. The oil giant recently announced that it has expanded its position in the country, as one of its joint ventures has been assigned rights to develop two adjacent oil fields. That supports Chevron's plans to invest more than $7 billion over the next five years to more than double its production in the country to around 600,000 barrels per day. The oil giant noted in the press release announcing its expanded position that the agreements include "enhanced fiscal, commercial, and legal terms intended to support durable and competitive long-term investments." That's something ExxonMobil investors should pay close attention to, because the company has previously said it needs durable investment protections and improved economics before it would commit to returning to Venezuela. The improved terms of Chevron's deal suggest that Venezuela appears willing to make the concessions that Exxon has been seeking as a condition of its return. While Trump's statement and Chevron's sweetened deal terms don't necessarily mean Exxon will return, they certainly hint at that to investors who are paying attention. Returning to Venezuela on improved terms would enhance Exxon's already strong plan to 2030, making it an even better oil stock to buy and hold long term.
